query: I am interested in high-entropy alloys for extreme temperature applications. How can we predict melting properties such as the melting temperature, entropy of fusion, and heat capacity for multi-component systems where experimental data is sparse or unreliable due to high melting points? I am looking for a hypothesis on a computational methodology that balances accuracy with the need to screen vast compositional spaces, along with prior evidence on why standard approaches struggle in this regime and what a valid boundary condition for such a method would be.

generation.hypothesis: A hybrid computational framework combining Cluster Expansion (CE) with the Quasi-Harmonic Approximation (QHA) and a machine-learned correction term trained on high-fidelity Density Functional Theory (DFT) data for binary and ternary subsystems will accurately predict the melting temperature, entropy of fusion, and heat capacity of refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) within 5% error, outperforming standard CALPHAD extrapolations and pure DFT calculations in both speed and accuracy for multi-component systems.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy system (e.g., W20Mo20Ta20Nb20V20 or HfNbTaTiZr) in a disordered body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solution state with a complex, multi-component composition space where experimental melting data is sparse or unreliable due to extreme melting points (>2000 K).
generation.intervention: Construct a Cluster Expansion model for the configurational energy of the alloy, parameterized using DFT calculations of ordered supercells derived from binary and ternary subsystems. Apply the Quasi-Harmonic Approximation to calculate vibrational free energy contributions up to the melting point. Integrate a Machine Learning (ML) correction term (e.g., Gaussian Process Regression or Neural Network) trained on the residuals between DFT-QHA predictions and available experimental data for known RHEAs to account for anharmonic effects and magnetic contributions not captured by standard QHA.
generation.conditions: Temperature range from 300 K to 2500 K (covering solid and near-melting states), pressure of 1 atm, and compositions within the high-entropy regime (5+ principal elements with near-equimolar ratios, specifically refractory metals like W, Mo, Ta, Nb, V).
generation.structural_mediator: The configurational entropy and vibrational phonon density of states, specifically the anharmonic phonon-phonon interactions and severe lattice distortion effects that become significant near the melting point in multi-component refractory systems.
generation.mechanism: Standard CALPHAD models struggle because they rely on extrapolation of binary/ternary parameters which often fail to capture the non-linear synergistic effects (e.g., severe lattice distortion, local chemical ordering) in high-entropy systems [PMC8282813::chunk::003::discussion::b590527e4b]. Pure DFT is too computationally expensive to sample the vast configurational space required for accurate melting point prediction via thermodynamic integration. The proposed method uses CE to efficiently map the configurational landscape, QHA to capture harmonic vibrational properties, and the ML correction to implicitly learn the missing anharmonic and magnetic physics from limited high-quality data, effectively bridging the gap between accuracy and computational cost.
generation.predicted_outcome: The hybrid CE-QHA-ML model will predict melting temperatures with a mean absolute error (MAE) of <50 K for novel RHEA compositions, whereas standard CALPHAD extrapolations will exhibit errors >150 K, and pure DFT methods will be computationally infeasible for screening >1000 compositions. The model will correctly predict the trend of entropy of fusion decreasing with increasing atomic size mismatch due to lattice distortion.
generation.baseline: Standard CALPHAD extrapolation using thermodynamic databases (e.g., Thermo-Calc) and pure DFT calculations using the harmonic approximation without anharmonic corrections or machine learning.
generation.boundary: The method is valid for substitutional solid solution RHEAs where the crystal structure remains BCC up to the melting point. It is not applicable to systems undergoing significant phase separation, intermetallic compound formation prior to melting (e.g., ordered B2 phases dominating the matrix), or where magnetic transitions dominate the thermodynamics in a way that cannot be captured by the training set's magnetic configurations [PMC5995863::chunk::000::abstract::63aa5c975c].
generation.uncertainty: The accuracy of the ML correction term is highly dependent on the diversity and quality of the training data; if the target HEA composition space is far from the binary/ternary subsystems used for training, the extrapolation error may increase. Additionally, the QHA may fail to accurately capture the pre-melting anharmonic softening in systems with very low Debye temperatures.

falsification_experiment.design: Select 10 novel refractory high-entropy alloy compositions not included in the training set. Perform the hybrid CE-QHA-ML prediction for their melting temperatures. Simultaneously, perform high-precision differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) or laser melting point measurements on these specific alloys.
measurements: Entropy of fusion (ΔSfus) via integration of heat capacity data
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the mean absolute error of the predicted melting temperatures exceeds 10% (or 150 K) for the 10 test compositions, or if the predicted trend of entropy of fusion contradicts the experimental trend in more than 50% of the test cases.

cited_evidence.text: Typically, refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), comprising a two-phase ordered B2 + BCC microstructure, exhibit extraordinarily high yield strengths, but poor ductility at room temperature, limiting their engineering application. The poor ductility is attributed to the continuous matrix being the ordered B2 phase in these alloys. This paper presents a novel approach to microstructural engineering of RHEAs to form an “inverted” BCC + B2 microstructure with discrete B2 precipitates dispersed within a continuous BCC matrix, resulting in improved room temperature compressive ductility, while maintaining high yield strength at both room and elevated temperature.

High entropy or multi principal element alloys are a promising and relatively young concept for designing alloys. The idea of creating alloys without a single main alloying element opens up a wide space for possible new alloy compositions. High entropy alloys based on refractory metals such as W, Mo, Ta or Nb are of interest for future high temperature applications e.g., in the aerospace or chemical industry. However, producing refractory metal high entropy alloys by conventional metallurgical methods remains challenging. For this reason, the feasibility of laser-based additive manufacturing of the refractory metal high entropy alloy W 20 Mo 20 Ta 20 Nb 20 V 20 by laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M) is investigated in the present work. In-situ alloy formation from mixtures of easily available elemental powders is employed to avoid an expensive atomization of pre-alloyed powder. It is shown that PBF-LB/M of W 20 Mo 20 Ta 20 Nb 20 V 20 is in general possible and that a complete fusion of the powder mixture without a significant number of undissolved particles is achievable by in-situ alloy formation during PBF-LB/M when selecting favorable process parameter combinations. High entropy alloys and related compositions are a relatively young concept for designing alloys. The formation of such multi component alloys was reported independently by Cantor et al. [ [1] ] and the research group around J.-W. Yeh in 2004 [ [2] , [3] , [4] ]. In contrast to most conventional alloys, high entropy alloys do not possess a single main alloying element but comprise a composition of multiple principal elements. The exact definition of high entropy alloys varies from source to source. The most common definition includes alloys consisting of at least five elements with a concentration between 5% and 35% each [ [5] ]. Other definitions demand a configurational entropy of at least 1.5 R [ [6] ]. However, both definitions are overlapping in large parts. Additionally, further criterions like the formation of a single phase solid solution were suggested [ [7] ]. These definitions are discussed extensively in recent review papers [ [7] ] and books [ [6] , [8] ]. The focus of the present work lies on the alloy W 20 Mo 20 Ta 20 Nb 20 V 20 , which is considered a high entropy alloy in agreement with all these criterions. The concept of HEAs provides us an unprecedented degree of freedom in the design of advanced alloys with promising properties. For the rapid exploration of the vast compositional space and investigation of the composition and temperature effects on the microstructure, advanced HEA-design strategies and efficient tools are necessary. At present, a few advanced HEA-design strategies were reported by combining the physicochemical criteria, CALPHAD, data mining, and multi-objective optimization algorithm [21] , [22] , [35] – [37] , demonstrating that the CALPHAD method has played an important role in the design of advanced HEAs. There are two essential requirements to carry out calculations, using the CALPHAD method: computational software and database.

The computational software could significantly affect the efficiency of HTC since massive calculations are carried out. In the example of the Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti quinary system, it takes only a few hours on a desktop computer to finish the HTCs (~ 3 × 10 3 ) within the composition range of 5–50 at.% for each element and finally screen out eight potential alloys.
